en: The Mahāyāna Śīla Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha,
translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, the Court Scattered Grandee, Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial,
and Great Master of the Transmission of the Dharma, the Subject Shi Hu, by Imperial Decree.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus, saying:

"There are those who destroy their moral conduct and shorten their lifespan, and there are those who sever their roots of goodness; it is difficult to encounter the life of one who has left the household life, so arouse a mind of diligence and guard it with firm resolve."

If any bhikṣus seek liberation within the Buddha-dharma, they should distance themselves from all evil and suffering; as the Buddha has taught, it would be better to sacrifice one's body and life to face impermanence than to indulge the mind and violate the precepts.
If a person loses their life, they merely destroy one lifetime; yet if they further break the precepts, they cause a million lifetimes to sink and wallow in the evil realms.
If a person upholds the precepts, they shall surely behold the Buddha.
Precepts are the supreme adornment; precepts are the most excellent fragrance; precepts are the superior cause of joy.
The essence of the precepts is pure, like clear, cool water, capable of removing the heat of affliction.
The Dharma of the precepts is supreme; even the worldly spells of dragons and serpents cannot harm one who observes them.
By upholding the precepts, one gains renown; by upholding the precepts, one attains peace and happiness. Thus, at the time of death, one shall further attain rebirth in the heavens.
The Buddha said: “Bhikṣus!

If one violates the code of discipline, it is like a blind person who cannot see various forms, or like one without feet who cannot travel the path; such a person remains far removed from nirvāṇa and fails to reach the other shore.”
If a person who upholds the precepts accomplishes all the treasures of the Dharma, they are like a noble vessel—perfect and solid—which can contain all manner of precious jewels.
If it is broken and damaged, the jewels will be lost;
likewise, if one breaks the code of discipline, one abandons all wholesome dharmas.
"If one has previously violated the precepts, yet later desires to seek nirvāṇa with such a mind, it is like trying to see one's face in a mirror after having had one's eyes and ears removed;
what capability could there possibly be? The Buddha said, "Bhikṣu!"
Women lack faith and should not be approached;
though a king’s favor may be great, it cannot be relied upon;
water bubbles have no substance and cannot be grasped.
Wealth and nobility are impermanent and cannot endure;
physical form is like a flower, subject to change in an instant;
life is like a ripe fruit that cannot remain long, like a boat crossing a swift current, or like a temporary stay in a dilapidated house.
"It would be better to consume poison than to drink alcohol;
it would be better to enter a great fire than to indulge in lustful desires!
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus and all the bodhisattvas were filled with great joy, and they faithfully accepted and practiced it.
The Mahāyāna Precepts Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha
